MUJAHID:v1p116#4/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p116#4/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v1p116#4/r1.claim: Mujahid says good things earned refers to trade.

MUQATIL:2:267/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:267/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:267/r1.claim: Believers should give good, lawful wealth, including gold, silver, and wholesome produce from the earth.

MUQATIL:2:267/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:267/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:267/r2.claim: Before the charity verse, a man gave a bunch of dates mostly made up of poor dates; the Prophet asked who brought it and had it hung up.

MUQATIL:2:267/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:267/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:267/r3.claim: Do not deliberately give poor dates as charity; people would not accept them for themselves at the price of good dates unless they waived some of their due.

MUQATIL:2:267/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:267/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:267/r4.claim: God is independent of people's wealth and praiseworthy in his dominion.

FARRA:v1p176/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p176/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p176/r1.claim: Different meanings allow adjacent ما ما or من من: the first ما can negate and the second be relative, while the first من can be interrogative and the second relative.

FARRA:v1p176/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p176/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p176/r2.claim: The poem كما ما امرؤ permits the two ما forms because the first is joined to ك as one unit and the second is separate; كلا لا وزر similarly joins one لا and leaves the next independent.

FARRA:v1p176/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p176/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p176/r3.claim: Exact particle repetition such as نعم نعم or اعجل اعجل is emphasis and differs from the two distinct grammatical cases.

FARRA:v1p176/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p176/r4.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p176/r4.claim: The second يوم in منذ يوم يوم means a known or understood day; بين بين means neither one group nor the other, like بيت بيت for adjoining houses.

MAJAZ:v1p82/r1.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p82/r1.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p82/r1.claim: Do not deliberately choose the inferior produce to give; Khafāf ibn Nadba's verse uses taya-mmamta for aiming at Mālik.

MAJAZ:v1p82/r2.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p82/r2.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p82/r2.claim: To accept it only by closing one's eyes means granting oneself a concession.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p108#3/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p108#3/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p108#3/r1.claim: Qatada forbids deliberately donating the worst of one's property; accepting it would require overlooking its defects or accepting a reduction.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p108#3/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p108#3/r2.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p108#3/r2.claim: He explains taking the bad item only by closing one's eyes as accepting it with a deduction.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p97#4/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p97#4/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p97#4/r1.claim: The good things earned means gold and silver, from which believers should give charity.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p97#4/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p97#4/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p97#4/r2.claim: The bad produce means poor-quality dates and goods the giver would accept only at a discount.

TAB-FULL:v4p694/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p694/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p694/r1.claim: The address is to those who believe in God, His messenger, and the signs of His Book; spending means paying zakat and giving charity.

TAB-FULL:v4p694/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p694/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p694/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the command to spend as giving charity.

TAB-FULL:v4p695/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p695/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p695/r1.claim: Give the good, lawful proceeds of trade or craft, especially high-quality gold and silver, rather than inferior goods in zakat.

TAB-FULL:v4p695/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p695/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v4p695/r2.claim: Mujāhid identifies the earnings as trade, specifically lawful trade.

TAB-FULL:v4p695/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p695/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن معقل
TAB-FULL:v4p695/r3.claim: Ibn Maʿqil says a believer's property contains nothing illicit, yet the verse still forbids deliberately giving its inferior portion.

TAB-FULL:v4p695/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p695/r4.speaker: علي
TAB-FULL:v4p695/r4.claim: ʿAlī identifies the earned goods here as gold and silver.

TAB-FULL:v4p695/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p695/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p695/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says to give from one's best and finest property.

TAB-FULL:v4p695/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p695/r6.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p695/r6.claim: Al-Suddī also identifies the earnings as gold and silver.

TAB-FULL:v4p697/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p697/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p697/r1.claim: The command includes zakat and charity from dates, grapes, wheat, barley, and every agricultural plant on which alms are due.

TAB-FULL:v4p697/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p697/r2.speaker: علي
TAB-FULL:v4p697/r2.claim: ʿAlī says the produce includes grain, fruit, and anything subject to zakat.

TAB-FULL:v4p697/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p697/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v4p697/r3.claim: Mujāhid identifies produce from the earth as dates or fruit from date palms.

TAB-FULL:v4p697/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p697/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v4p697/r4.claim: A second report from Mujāhid specifies fruit from date palms.

TAB-FULL:v4p697/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p697/r5.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p697/r5.claim: Al-Suddī says the verse concerns dates and grain.

TAB-FULL:v4p698/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p698/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p698/r1.claim: Tayammum means to deliberately aim for or choose something.

TAB-FULL:v4p698/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p698/r2.speaker: الأعشى
TAB-FULL:v4p698/r2.claim: Al-Aʿshā's line provides poetic evidence that the verb means to intend or aim at.

TAB-FULL:v4p698/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p698/r3.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p698/r3.claim: Al-Suddī glosses the command as do not deliberately choose the inferior.

TAB-FULL:v4p698/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p698/r4.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v4p698/r4.claim: Qatāda also glosses it as do not deliberately choose.

TAB-FULL:v4p698/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p698/r5.speaker: البراء بن عازب
TAB-FULL:v4p698/r5.claim: Al-Barāʾ reports that some Anṣār mixed spoiled dates into the fruit hung for poor emigrants at the Prophet's mosque, thinking it acceptable; the verse forbade this.

TAB-FULL:v4p701/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p701/r1.speaker: البراء بن عازب
TAB-FULL:v4p701/r1.claim: A further report from al-Barāʾ says people brought their worst dates and food for charity, prompting the verse.

TAB-FULL:v4p701/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p701/r2.speaker: علي
TAB-FULL:v4p701/r2.claim: ʿAlī says the verse concerns obligatory zakat: people kept good dates and paid the zakat collector with inferior ones.

TAB-FULL:v4p701/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p701/r3.speaker: أبو أمامة بن سهل بن حنيف
TAB-FULL:v4p701/r3.claim: Abū Umāma identifies the disallowed dates as the varieties jaʿrūr and ḥubayq; the Prophet forbade taking them for charity.

TAB-FULL:v4p701/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p701/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v4p701/r4.claim: Mujāhid says people gave rotten and inferior dates from their palms and were ordered to give the good ones.

TAB-FULL:v4p701/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p701/r5.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v4p701/r5.claim: Qatāda says a man with two orchards selected the worse dates and mixed in spoiled ones, which God condemned.

TAB-FULL:v4p702/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p702/r1.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v4p702/r1.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the verse came down because people gave the inferior portion of their property.

TAB-FULL:v4p702/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p702/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v4p702/r2.claim: Mujāhid describes spoiled dates noticed among the hanging clusters; the Prophet asked what they were.

TAB-FULL:v4p702/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p702/r3.speaker: عطاء
TAB-FULL:v4p702/r3.claim: ʿAṭāʾ reports that after someone hung spoiled dates, the Prophet condemned it and the verse was revealed.

TAB-FULL:v4p702/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p702/r4.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v4p702/r4.claim: Ibn Zayd offers an alternative: khabīth means illicit property, which God does not accept.

TAB-FULL:v4p702/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p702/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p702/r5.claim: Al-Ṭabarī rejects Ibn Zayd's illicit-property reading in favor of the interpretation reported from the Companions and shared by exegetes: inferior-quality goods.

TAB-FULL:v4p704/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p704/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p704/r1.claim: The pronoun refers to inferior goods; recipients would accept them only by relinquishing part of their due right.

TAB-FULL:v4p704/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p704/r2.speaker: الطرماح بن حكيم
TAB-FULL:v4p704/r2.claim: Al-Ṭirimmāḥ's use of الإغماض supports its sense of tolerating a shortfall or waiving part of one's right.

TAB-FULL:v4p704/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p704/r3.speaker: علي
TAB-FULL:v4p704/r3.claim: ʿAlī says a person would not accept inferior repayment unless the debtor discounted it.

TAB-FULL:v4p704/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p704/r4.speaker: البراء بن عازب
TAB-FULL:v4p704/r4.claim: Al-Barāʾ says a creditor would reject this payment unless he saw that his right had been reduced.

TAB-FULL:v4p704/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p704/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p704/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says people would not accept inferior goods for a full debt and asks how they can offer God what they reject; he links this to 3:92.

TAB-FULL:v4p704/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p704/r6.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v4p704/r6.claim: Mujāhid says one would accept inferior goods from debtors or in sales only if given extra beyond the amount of good goods.

TAB-FULL:v4p705/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p705/r1.speaker: الربيع
TAB-FULL:v4p705/r1.claim: Al-Rabīʿ says one would take an inferior debt payment only reluctantly, knowing it fell short of the due amount.

TAB-FULL:v4p705/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p705/r2.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v4p705/r2.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says hypocrites paid obligatory zakat with their worst food, which recipients would accept only while aware of the shortfall.

TAB-FULL:v4p705/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p705/r3.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v4p705/r3.claim: Al-Ḥasan says one would buy inferior goods at the market only after the seller reduced their price.

TAB-FULL:v4p705/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p705/r4.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v4p705/r4.claim: Qatāda says inferior goods would be accepted at the price of good goods only if the price were reduced.

TAB-FULL:v4p705/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p705/r5.speaker: البراء بن عازب
TAB-FULL:v4p705/r5.claim: Al-Barāʾ says even as a gift people would accept such goods only out of embarrassment or resentment toward the giver.

TAB-FULL:v4p708/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p708/r1.speaker: ابن معقل
TAB-FULL:v4p708/r1.claim: Ibn Maʿqil interprets the phrase as accepting inferior repayment only if one waives part of one's due right.

TAB-FULL:v4p708/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p708/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v4p708/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd gives another interpretation: one accepts illicit property only while knowingly overlooking its sin.

TAB-FULL:v4p708/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p708/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p708/r3.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers the due-right interpretation: zakat recipients own a share of the good wealth, so the payer cannot substitute inferior goods for their proportionate share.

TAB-FULL:v4p708/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p708/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p708/r4.claim: For voluntary charity, he does not forbid giving less than the very best, since a larger or more useful lesser-quality gift may benefit its recipient more.

TAB-FULL:v4p710/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p710/r1.speaker: عبيدة
TAB-FULL:v4p710/r1.claim: ʿUbayda says the rule concerns obligatory zakat; a counterfeit dirham is preferable to a date as payment, while voluntary charity may be less than the best.

TAB-FULL:v4p711/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p711/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p711/r1.claim: God needs no charity; He imposed it out of mercy to support dependents and the weak and to increase people's afterlife reward.

TAB-FULL:v4p711/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p711/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p711/r2.claim: God is praised by His creatures for His blessings and generosity toward them.

TAB-FULL:v4p711/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p711/r3.speaker: البراء بن عازب
TAB-FULL:v4p711/r3.claim: Al-Barāʾ glosses God's being rich and praiseworthy as independence from people's charity.

ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r4.claim: Give good earnings from trade, gold or silver, and good produce; some people had offered inferior dates as charity.

ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r5.speaker: النبي
ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r5.claim: A report says the Prophet instructed collectors not to assess two inferior date varieties, so donors would not use them as an excuse for giving bad produce.

ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r1.claim: Do not deliberately choose inferior goods for charity when you would accept them only at a discount.

ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r2.claim: God is self-sufficient and praiseworthy; He did not command charity from need but as a test, and is praised for that and all His blessings.

ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r3.claim: The verb ġaniya means to be self-sufficient; the noun maghnā can denote a protected dwelling place, and ghina can mean skillful song.

ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r4.speaker: قيس بن الخطيم
ZAJJAJ:v1p350/r4.claim: Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm’s line uses ghinyān for a woman’s singing; ghawānī may name women because they are rich in beauty or have husbands.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p525/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p525/r1.speaker: الزهري
IBNABIHATIM:v2p525/r1.claim: Al-Zuhri says that when God addresses “O you who believe,” the Prophet is included among the believers.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p525/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p525/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p525/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets “spend” as “give charity”; Muqatil is reported to agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p525/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p525/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p525/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says “the good things you have earned” means your best and most wholesome possessions; al-Zuhri is reported to agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p525/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p525/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p525/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Companions used to buy cheap food to give in charity, so God revealed this command to give from good earnings.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r1.claim: Mujahid first interprets produce from the earth as dates from palm trees, some of which people had been giving as inferior dates; they were told to give good produce instead.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r2.claim: Mujahid has a second reported interpretation of produce from the earth as plants, differing from his first interpretation as palm trees.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r3.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r3.claim: Muqatil interprets produce from the earth as fruits, dates, raisins, grapes, and grain.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r4.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r4.claim: Al-Bara ibn Azib glosses “do not deliberately seek” as “do not intend.”

IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r5.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r5.claim: Al-Bara says the bad produce people should not deliberately give is inferior dried dates.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r6.speaker: عبد الله بن معقل
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r6.claim: Ibn Ma'qil says a Muslim's earnings are not intrinsically bad, but one should not give inferior dates, counterfeit coins, or worthless property.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r7.speaker: عبيدة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p527/r7.claim: Ubayda says the verse concerns obligatory zakat; for voluntary charity, even a date is acceptable, and a counterfeit coin is better than a date. A conflicting report from him is noted without its content.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r1.speaker: عبيدة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r1.claim: Ubayda identifies the bad goods people should not donate as counterfeit dirhams and similar items.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r2.speaker: سهل بن حنيف
IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r2.claim: Sahl reports that the Prophet forbade two inferior date varieties because people were selecting their worst dates for charity, prompting this verse.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r3.speaker: البراء
IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r3.claim: Al-Bara recounts that some date growers donated rotten or broken clusters; the verse came, and afterward people brought their better dates.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas compares donating inferior goods to repaying a creditor less than owed, which one would accept only after discounting; God is owed one's best wealth.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r5.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v2p528/r5.claim: Hasan says people would not buy such goods in the market unless their price were reduced.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p529/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن معقل
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529/r1.claim: Ibn Muqill glosses accepting an inferior donation with lowered expectations as tolerating it.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p529/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529/r2.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529/r2.claim: Al-Bara says God is independent of people's alms.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p529/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529/r3.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
IBNABIHATIM:v2p529/r3.claim: Muqatil explains God's being rich as His sovereign independence from what people possess.

NAHHAS:v1p335/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p335/r2.speaker: عبد الله
NAHHAS:v1p335/r2.claim: Abd Allah reads ولا تأمموا; Ibn Kathir reads ولا تيمموا by assimilation, and Qatada interprets إلا أن تغمضوا as a discounted price.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p138/r1.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p138/r1.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p138/r1.claim: The pattern فعْلان generally signals motion or lightness in descriptions and verbal nouns, though examples such as صفوان show that it can also occur in ordinary nouns.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p138/r2.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p138/r2.speaker: الزهري ومسلم بن جندب
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p138/r2.claim: Al-Zuhrī and Muslim ibn Jundub read ولا تَيَمَّموا with ḍamma on tāʾ and kasra on mīm; its several verb forms all mean to intend or seek.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p138/r3.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p138/r3.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p138/r3.claim: The root أ م م means intending; الإمام is what one aims at or relies on, and الأمة can mean an intended path, as in the cited verse.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p139/r1.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p139/r1.speaker: الأصمعي
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p139/r1.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī reports the form غار for 'sank or disappeared'; the source says this sense differs from the interpretation that means going to al-Ghawr.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p139/r2.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p139/r2.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p139/r2.claim: The form تغمضوا can be transferred from intransitive غمض to transitive أغمضه, meaning that someone else causes the overlooking.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p139/r4.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p139/r4.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p139/r4.claim: On the transferred reading, the wording can mean finding people treating the poor offering as something they have already overlooked, supported by other examples of أفعل meaning 'find in a state.'

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p140/r1.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p140/r1.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p140/r1.claim: Another sense of تغمضوا is to be drawn toward the inferior gift by desire until it seems acceptable; al-Zuhrī's report can mean deliberately closing one's judgment to its defect.

THALABI:v2p265/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p265/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p265/r7.claim: “Good things” means the choice and finest portions of what one has earned, in line with the command to spend what one loves.

THALABI:v2p265/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p265/r8.speaker: ابن مسعود ومجاهد
THALABI:v2p265/r8.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid interpret ṭayyibāt here as lawful goods, supported by the commands to the messengers and believers to eat from the good things.

THALABI:v2p266/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p266/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p266/r1.claim: The verse addressed to believers to eat from the good provisions supports interpreting ṭayyibāt as lawful, good earnings.

THALABI:v2p266/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p266/r10.speaker: سعيد بن عمير
THALABI:v2p266/r10.claim: Saʿīd ibn ʿUmayr reports that the best livelihood is a man's work by his own hand and every fair sale.

THALABI:v2p266/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p266/r11.speaker: محمد بن الراضبي
THALABI:v2p266/r11.claim: Muḥammad al-Rāḍibī recounts Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī saying that spinning is among good provisions, citing ʿAlī.

THALABI:v2p266/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p266/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v2p266/r2.claim: A prophetic report says God accepts only what is good: charity from unlawful wealth is not accepted, its owner is not blessed by spending it, and it becomes provision for Hell; evil is not erased by evil.

THALABI:v2p266/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p266/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p266/r3.claim: “What you have earned” includes wealth made through trade and craft, such as gold and silver.

THALABI:v2p266/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p266/r4.speaker: عبيد بن رفاعة
THALABI:v2p266/r4.claim: ʿUbayd ibn Rifāʿah reports the Prophet calling merchants sinful except those who are pious, dutiful, and truthful.

THALABI:v2p266/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p266/r5.speaker: قيس بن عروة الغفاري
THALABI:v2p266/r5.claim: Qays ibn ʿUrwah al-Ghifārī says the Prophet renamed brokers as traders and told them to offset the distractions, lies, and oaths of selling with charity.

THALABI:v2p266/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p266/r6.speaker: مكحول عن أبي أمامة
THALABI:v2p266/r6.claim: Makhūl reports from Abū Umāmah a saying that trade is the best of ten shares of livelihood when the trader gives and takes what is right, and another report says nine tenths of provision is in trade.

THALABI:v2p266/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p266/r7.speaker: ابن جريج عن عطاء عن ابن عباس
THALABI:v2p266/r7.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās urges Quraysh not to let their non-Arab clients surpass them in trade, praises its blessing, and warns against an oath-swearing, base merchant.

THALABI:v2p266/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p266/r8.speaker: عاصم ابن أبي النجود عن أبي وائل
THALABI:v2p266/r8.claim: Abū Wāʾil says a dirham earned in trade is dearer to him than ten dirhams from his stipend.

THALABI:v2p266/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p266/r9.speaker: الأعمش عن أبي إبراهيم عن عائشة
THALABI:v2p266/r9.claim: ʿĀʾishah reports the Prophet saying that the best food a man eats comes from his own earnings, and his child is part of his earnings.

THALABI:v2p267/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p267/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p267/r1.claim: Produce from the earth means staple, storable grains and fruits on which zakat is due.

THALABI:v2p267/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p267/r10.speaker: باذان عن ابن عباس
THALABI:v2p267/r10.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports the Prophet saying that God has a due in people's property, to be paid when it reaches the required amount; people brought charity to the mosque for him to distribute.

THALABI:v2p267/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p267/r2.speaker: عمر بن دينار عن جابر بن عبد الله
THALABI:v2p267/r2.claim: Jābir reports that the Prophet said whoever plants a tree receives charity for every person, animal, or bird that eats from it until the Resurrection.

THALABI:v2p267/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p267/r3.speaker: هشام بن عروة عن أبيه عن عائشة
THALABI:v2p267/r3.claim: ʿĀʾishah reports the Prophet advising people to seek provision in the hidden places of the earth.

THALABI:v2p267/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p267/r4.speaker: مالك بن دينار
THALABI:v2p267/r4.claim: Mālik ibn Dīnār says he read in the Torah a blessing for one who eats the fruit of his own hands.

THALABI:v2p267/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p267/r5.speaker: ابن مسعود
THALABI:v2p267/r5.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads the command with hamza as taʾammamū; Ibn ʿAbbās reads it with a different vowel pattern, both meaning “aim for.”

THALABI:v2p267/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p267/r6.speaker: ابن كثير
THALABI:v2p267/r6.claim: Ibn Kathīr doubles the yāʾ in tayammamū at this and thirty other places, contracting the original two tāʾs; other readers use the light form.

THALABI:v2p267/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p267/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p267/r7.claim: The forms amamtu, tayammamtu, and taʾammamtu all mean to intend or aim; a line by al-Aʿshā witnesses tayammamtu.

THALABI:v2p267/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p267/r8.speaker: السدي عن علي بن ثابت عن الفراء
THALABI:v2p267/r8.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reports that the verse addressed Anṣār who hung date clusters in the Prophet's mosque for poor emigrants; some chose clusters of rotten dates, thinking the abundance excused it.

THALABI:v2p267/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p267/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p267/r9.claim: The bad gift is a cluster containing rotten dates, which the giver would not accept if it were offered to him.

THALABI:v2p268/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p268/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p268/r1.claim: A report says a man placed a cluster of rotten dates into the charity after worshippers had dispersed; the Prophet condemned the donor, and the verse was revealed.

THALABI:v2p268/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p268/r2.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب والحسن ومجاهد والضحاك
THALABI:v2p268/r2.claim: ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say people gave the worst of their fruit and property while keeping the good; examples include rotten dates, spoiled grain, and debased coins.

THALABI:v2p268/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p268/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p268/r3.claim: The syntax of illa an tughmiḍū fīhi has an omitted preposition and means “unless you overlook it.”

THALABI:v2p268/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p268/r4.speaker: الزهري والحسن وقتادة وأبو مجلن
THALABI:v2p268/r4.claim: Al-Zuhrī, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, and Abū Mujlaz transmit different vowelings of tughmiḍū; the readings represent recognized dialect forms.

THALABI:v2p268/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p268/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p268/r5.claim: Ighmāḍ literally means lowering the gaze or closing one eyelid over the other, then came to mean tolerating or relaxing one's standards in a sale.

THALABI:v2p268/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p268/r6.speaker: علي والبراء بن عازب
THALABI:v2p268/r6.claim: ʿAlī and al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib explain the verse as a creditor's reluctance to accept an inferior item except by overlooking part of his right; al-ʿAwfī transmits this from Ibn ʿAbbās.

THALABI:v2p268/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p268/r7.speaker: الولبي عن ابن عباس
THALABI:v2p268/r7.claim: Al-Wālibī reports Ibn ʿAbbās explaining that one would not accept the poor item at the value of good produce without reducing what was owed.

THALABI:v2p268/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p268/r8.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
THALABI:v2p268/r8.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah say buyers would only accept such produce in the market at a reduced price, not the price of good produce.

THALABI:v2p268/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p268/r9.speaker: الفراء
THALABI:v2p268/r9.claim: Al-Farrāʾ adds that a person would accept the defective item as a gift only with embarrassment and annoyance; people should not offer God what they reject for themselves.

THALABI:v2p269/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p269/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p269/r1.claim: Recipients of zakat share in the owner's property: when all of it is good, they share in the good; if it is all poor quality, paying that is permissible unless the giver voluntarily improves it.

THALABI:v2p269/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p269/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p269/r2.claim: God is independent of people's spending and charity, and praised in His acts.

THALABI:v2p269/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p269/r3.speaker: معبد بن منقذ عن أبي شريح الكعبي
THALABI:v2p269/r3.claim: Abū Shurayḥ al-Kaʿbī says to rebuke him as insane if people see him giving away the worst of what he owns.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r1.speaker: علي
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r1.claim: Ali interprets the good things earned as gold and silver; other views identify them as trade, lawful property, or good-quality property.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r10.speaker: ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r10.claim: Ibn Zayd interprets the rejected inferior property as unlawful wealth.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r11.speaker: البراء بن عازب
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r11.claim: The exception for taking such property only with closed eyes means being lenient about it, according to al-Bara.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r12.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the phrase as accepting a deduction from the price.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r13.speaker: الزجاج
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r13.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains the exception as giving it only at a discount, and al-Suddi as lowering its value for oneself.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r14.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r14.speaker: السدي
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r14.claim: Al-Suddi says people would only take such inferior goods by allowing themselves a bargain price; al-Tirimmih's verse witnesses the expression al-ighmad.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r2.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r2.claim: Mujahid says the good things earned means trade.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r3.claim: Other interpretations take the good earnings to mean lawful property or the best-quality property.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r4.claim: What God produces from the earth refers to crops and fruits.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r5.claim: Earnings may mean newly acquired wealth or all property owned, old and new.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r6.speaker: عبيدة السلماني
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r6.claim: Ubayda al-Salmani says this spending is obligatory alms; some theologians say it is voluntary charity.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r7.speaker: الخليل
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r7.claim: Al-Khalil defines tayammum as deliberate intent, distinguishing amam, heading in front, from yammam, deliberately aiming from any direction; another view treats the two as equivalent.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r8.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r8.claim: Al-khabith means inferior or poor quality in anything; one view says collectors mixed poor dates into charity dates, while Ibn Zayd says it means unlawful property.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r9.speaker: علي والبراء بن عازب
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p342/r9.claim: Ali and al-Bara ibn Azib say people brought poor-quality dates and mixed them into the charity collection.

QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r4.claim: Each giver should examine what he offers for his own sake and what he gives at his Lord’s command.

QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r5.claim: What is kept for oneself is often treated as a precious possession, while what is offered to God should be chosen from one’s finest property.

QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r6.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r6.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p123/r6.claim: Everything comes from God, yet He accepts and repays the gift, credits the act to the giver, and calls His own generous provision a reward.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p87/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p87/r4.speaker: جابر
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p87/r4.claim: Jābir reports that after a man brought poor-quality dates for the prescribed fitr charity, this command to give from good earnings was revealed.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p87/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p87/r5.speaker: البراء
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p87/r5.claim: Al-Barāʾ says the Anṣār hung clusters of dates and unripe dates in the Prophet’s mosque for poor emigrants to eat.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p89/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p89/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p89/r1.claim: The account concludes that some men deliberately donated clusters containing rotten dates, thinking the gift acceptable amid the many better clusters; the verse forbids choosing such produce.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r1.claim: “Good things” can mean the finest assets or lawful earnings from trade and craft, including gold and silver.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r2.claim: What God brings from the earth means grains on which zakat is due.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r3.claim: Tayammum means deliberate intent or aim; the source cites several Arabic verb forms and poetic examples.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r4.claim: Most readers lighten the second تاء by dropping one of two; Ibn Kathir assimilates them and reads it with a doubled تاء.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r5.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r5.claim: He argues the doubled reading should not be possible: assimilation leaves a consonant needing initial hamzat al-waṣl, which does not enter a present-tense verb; an assimilating reader must begin with the light form.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r6.speaker: هشام
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r6.claim: He says the first of the two تاء letters is omitted in the common reading.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r7.speaker: الفراء وسيبويه
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r7.claim: Al-Farra says either تاء may be dropped because the remaining one substitutes for it; Sībawayh says only the second is dropped.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p422/r8.claim: A man brought a date cluster of inferior dates to charity; the Prophet asked what its donor had done, and the verse was revealed.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r1.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r1.claim: They say people used to donate the worst fruit and poorest property, so the verse was revealed; الخبيث means inferior property.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r2.claim: Here الخبيث means the bad or low-quality portion of one's property.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r3.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r3.claim: He takes أن after إلا as conditional: if you tolerate the defect somewhat, you take it; it can be paraphrased “only through lenience,” with parallels in 2:229 and 2:237.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r4.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r4.claim: He rejects the conditional account: أن with a verb as a verbal noun is always open, and the verse means one accepts it only by tolerating its defect.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r5.claim: Ighmāḍ literally means lowering or closing the eye, from concealment; figuratively it means overlooking a defect or showing lenience in a sale.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r6.claim: Ighmid lī fī al-bayʿa means increase the amount or lower the price because the item is defective; if one accepts bad goods only at a discount, how can one donate them?

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r7.speaker: ابن عباس في رواية العوفي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p424/r7.claim: If a creditor were repaid with inferior goods, he would accept only if he thought the debtor had discounted or forgiven part of the debt.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r1.speaker: ابن عباس في رواية الوالبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r1.claim: One would not accept the defective item at the price of a good one unless the price were reduced; al-Hasan and Qatada share this interpretation.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r2.claim: This interpretation takes the verb causatively: you make the seller lower the price or overlook the defect, with its object omitted; Abu Mujliz's passive reading supports “unless it is discounted for you.”

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r3.speaker: فريق من أصحاب النظم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r3.claim: One parsing ends the first clause at ولا تيمموا الخبيث; a new clause means “you spend from it,” and you would not accept such goods when owed except through lenience. The participle الآخذون stands for a verb.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r4.speaker: الفريق الثاني من أصحاب النظم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r4.claim: The other parsing runs through إلا أن تغمضوا فيه, with الذي understood: do not choose the bad portion that you spend, which you would accept only by tolerating it.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r5.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p427/r5.claim: The needy share in the owner's property; if his stock is good, they share in its good portion, since a partner would not accept inferior goods from good stock without lenience.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r4.claim: The verse was revealed about people who gave charity from their worst fruits and lowest-quality possessions.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r5.claim: The good things to give are the best goods earned through trade and the grains from the earth on which zakat is due.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r6.claim: Do not deliberately choose inferior goods: you would accept them for your own rights only grudgingly or by overlooking their defects, since the poor share the owner's wealth.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r7.claim: The poor are partners in the owner's property, and a partner accepts inferior goods only by leniency.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r1.speaker: ابن مسعود ومجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r1.claim: Ibn Masud and Mujahid say the 'good things' to spend are lawful earnings from trade and craft; the verse indicates earnings may be wholesome or corrupt.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r2.speaker: عائشة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r2.claim: Aisha reports the Prophet saying that the best food a man eats is from his own earnings, and his child counts among his earnings.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r3.speaker: المقدام بن معد يكرب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r3.claim: Al-Miqdam reports the Prophet saying no food is better than what one earns by hand; David also ate only from his own labor.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r4.claim: Ibn Masud reports that unlawful wealth given in charity is not accepted or blessed and becomes provision for the Fire if left behind; evil is not erased by evil.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329#2/r5.claim: Most scholars require annual zakat on trade goods at one quarter of a tenth of their value, once worth twenty dinars or two hundred dirhams; Samura says the Prophet ordered zakat on goods held for sale.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r1.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r1.claim: Umar treated the hides Himas carried, which he said were his only goods for tanning, as taxable trade property and collected their zakat.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r2.claim: The produce clause requires a tenth on dates, grapes, and staple grains irrigated by rain or a naturally flowing river; costly irrigation reduces it to a half-tenth.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r3.speaker: ابن عمر
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r3.claim: Ibn Umar reports the Prophetic rule: naturally watered or rain-fed crops owe a tenth, while crops watered by irrigation equipment owe half that.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r4.speaker: عتاب بن أسيد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r4.claim: Attab ibn Asid reports the Prophet's instruction to assess grapes as date palms are assessed, then pay the grape zakat as raisins, just as palm zakat is paid in dates.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r5.speaker: ابن أبي ليلى والشافعي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r5.claim: Ibn Abi Layla and al-Shafii say no tithe is due on crops outside dates, grapes, and staple grains.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r6.speaker: الزهري والأوزاعي ومالك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r6.claim: Al-Zuhri, al-Awzai, and Malik require zakat on olives.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r7.speaker: أبو حنيفة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r7.claim: Abu Hanifa requires a tithe on all vegetables and fruits except grass and firewood.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r8.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r8.claim: For fruit, liability begins when it ripens and payment follows harvest and drying; for grain, it begins when firm and is paid after threshing and cleaning.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r9.speaker: أكثر أهل العلم وأبو حنيفة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p330/r9.claim: Most scholars require the five-wasq threshold, while Abu Hanifa requires zakat on any amount; the author cites a hadith setting thresholds for dates, silver, and camels.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r1.claim: A report from Abu Said says no zakat is due on grain or dates until they reach five wasqs; some say this verse concerns voluntary charity instead.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r2.speaker: أنس بن مالك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r2.claim: Anas reports the Prophet saying that when a believer plants a tree or crop and a person, bird, or animal eats from it, the believer receives charity's reward.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r3.claim: Ibn Kathir's al-Bazzi doubles the t in tayammamu in connected recitation at 31 Qur'anic locations; other readers use the lighter form, meaning do not deliberately choose.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r4.claim: Some Ansar hung date bunches in the Prophet's mosque for poor emigrants, and a man added a bunch of inferior dates thinking the abundance made it acceptable; others regularly set aside their worst fruit for charity.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r5.claim: Ighmad means making an allowance: one would accept inferior property only by overlooking one's full due; al-Hasan and Qatada say one would not pay the good price for it in a market.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r6.speaker: البراء
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r6.claim: Al-Bara says a person would accept such inferior produce as a gift only with embarrassment and annoyance, so donors should not give others what they would not accept themselves.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r7.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r7.claim: If one's wealth is all good, one may not give the inferior portion because eligible recipients share in one's holdings; if all of it is inferior, it may be given.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r8.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p332/r8.claim: God is independent of people's charity and praiseworthy in His actions.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r1.claim: The good things earned means the finest of one's earnings.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r10.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r10.speaker: قتادة
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r10.claim: Qatada's passive reading means being compelled to accept or to be found accepting it with one's eyes shut.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r11.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r11.speaker: الحسن
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r11.claim: Al-Hasan says one would not buy such goods at market unless their price were reduced.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r12.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r12.claim: Ibn Abbas says they used to give the worst dates, and were forbidden to do so.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r2.claim: What God brings from the earth includes grain, fruit, minerals, and other products.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r3.claim: The phrase ‘good things’ is omitted before what comes from the earth because the preceding mention already supplies it.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r4.claim: Do not deliberately select inferior wealth to spend, specifying it as the item for charity.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r5.claim: Abdullah and Ibn Abbas have variant readings of ولا تيمموا; the forms yimma, tayammama, and taʾammama all mean to intend.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r6.claim: You would not accept such inferior wealth in settling your own rights.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r7.claim: Overlooking it means tolerating it as payment; the metaphor comes from lowering one's gaze, and merchants say not to insist on full value.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r8.speaker: الطرماح
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r8.claim: Al-Tirimmāḥ's verse attests to accepting injury or deficiency by overlooking it.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r9.speaker: الزهري
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p342/r9.claim: Al-Zuhri read تغمضوا; variants أغمض and غمض have the same meaning, and another vocalization is reported.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r1.claim: The address and command to give apply to the whole community of Muhammad.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r10.speaker: عبد الله بن مغفل
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r10.claim: He supports the broad reading by saying a believer's property contains nothing vile.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r11.claim: Earnings include bodily labor and trade, and inheritances count because the human or believing community acquired them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r12.claim: What God brings forth from the earth includes plants, minerals, buried treasure, and similar things.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r2.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب، عبيدة السلماني، محمد بن سيرين
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r2.claim: They take the command as obligatory zakat: do not substitute poor quality for good; voluntary gifts may be small or modest in value.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r3.speaker: البراء بن عازب، الحسن بن أبي الحسن، قتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r3.claim: They understand the verse as voluntary charity, for which the command recommends rather than obliges giving good-quality goods.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r4.speaker: البراء بن عازب، عطاء بن أبي رباح
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r4.claim: They report that Ansar hung date clusters in the mosque for poor emigrants; after a man hung dry, poor dates, the Prophet condemned it and the verse was revealed.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r5.claim: The verse covers both obligatory zakat and voluntary charity: the former makes giving good obligatory, the latter makes it recommended.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r6.speaker: جمهور المتأولين
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r6.claim: Most interpreters take tayyib as good, choice property and khabith as inferior or base property.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r7.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r7.claim: Ibn Zayd reads tayyib as lawful earnings and khabith as forbidden property.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r8.claim: Ibn Zayd's interpretation is weak in the verse's syntactic sequence, though it is not intrinsically impossible.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361#2/r9.claim: Tayyib may simply mean what you have earned, with its mention praising the quality and blessing of earnings and encompassing both good quality and lawful origin.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r1.claim: The debt and market-price explanations fit the verse's application to obligatory zakat.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r10.claim: Alternatively the word evokes closing one's eyes to something unpleasant, as in another poet's line and the related term al-ighḍāʾ.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r11.claim: A further possibility derives from going to a remote or obscure place, like the verbs for going to Oman, Iraq, Najd, or the lowlands.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r12.claim: The majority reading can mean tolerating, closing one's eyes, or resorting to obscure interpretation when accepting the property, including forbidden, gifted, or owed property under the reported views.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r13.speaker: أبو عمرو
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r13.claim: He explains al-Zuhri's first reading as reducing the seller's asking price; both al-Zuhri readings can mean taking it at a discount.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r2.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r2.claim: He also explains the phrase as reluctance to accept an unwanted gift unless one overlooks its poor value, fitting voluntary charity.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd takes the phrase to mean that one would accept forbidden property only by overlooking its repugnance.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r4.claim: The majority reads tuġmiḍū with ḍamma on tāʾ, a still ghayn, and kasra on mīm.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r5.speaker: الزهري
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r5.claim: Al-Zuhri's first reading has fatḥa on tāʾ and a light kasra on mīm; he also transmits a doubled-mīm form with ḍamma on tāʾ.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r6.speaker: الحسن البصري، مكي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r6.claim: Makkī transmits al-Hasan's form with doubled and open mīm and open tāʾ.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r7.speaker: قتادة، أبو عمرو
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r7.claim: Qatada reads with open mīm, and Abu Amr glosses the construction as accepting it only when it is discounted for you.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r8.claim: The expression can derive from a verb meaning to tolerate, waive part of one's due, and accept less than one's full right.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r9.speaker: الطرماح بن حكيم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362#2/r9.claim: His verse uses al-ighmāḍ for accepting lenient terms and tolerating a shortfall.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r1.claim: Tayammamu means deliberately to intend or aim at something; two cited poems attest this usage.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r10.claim: The connected construction makes tunfiqūn function as a circumstantial accusative, like saying one goes out only to strive in God's path.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r11.speaker: البراء بن عازب، ابن عباس، الضحاك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r11.claim: They explain the verse as property owed in debts or rights: one would accept inferior property only by reluctantly waiving part of one's due, so one should not offer God what one dislikes.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r12.speaker: الحسن بن أبي الحسن
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r12.claim: He says a buyer would accept such goods in the market only if the seller reduced their price.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r13.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r13.claim: A similar explanation is transmitted from Ali: one accepts it only after a reduction in its price.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r2.claim: The majority reads tayammamu; al-Bazzi transmits gemination of the initial tā from Ibn Kathir in thirty-one places, beginning here.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r3.claim: A transmitted reading says la tuʾimmu al-khabīth, using the verb for intending; its meaning matches the standard reading.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r4.speaker: الزهري، مسلم بن جندب
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r4.claim: They read the verb with ḍamma on tāʾ and kasra on mīm, following the dialect that says yammamtu for intending.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r5.claim: The word has forms with light or doubled mīm and with or without the initial tāʾ, all expressing intention.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r6.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود، أبو عمرو
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r6.claim: Another transmitted form is tuʾammamu, with a hamza after tāʾ, reflecting the form with doubled mīm.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r7.speaker: الجرجاني
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r7.claim: One syntactic analysis ends the sentence at al-khabīth and begins a new description: people spend that vile property though they would accept it only reluctantly.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r8.claim: On that analysis, the clause rebukes people, and the pronoun in minhu refers to the vile property.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r9.speaker: الجرجاني
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p362/r9.claim: A second analysis keeps the syntax connected through fīhi, referring minhu to what was earned and taking tunfiqūn as a circumstantial clause.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r1.speaker: أبو عمرو الداني
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r1.claim: Al-Dani's account explains al-Zuhri's second reading; Ibn Atiyya also allows that it may refer to closing the eyes.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r2.speaker: أبو عمرو
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r2.claim: Abu Amr's explanation of Qatada's reading was given above.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r3.speaker: ابن جني
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r3.claim: Ibn Jinni takes Qatada's form to mean that people are found to have overlooked or interpreted the matter leniently, like finding someone praiseworthy.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r4.claim: God is self-sufficient and has no need of charity; those seeking closeness and reward should give what is valuable.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p363/r5.claim: Ḥamīd means praised in every state and is an essential attribute.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:267#2/r1.claim: The preceding phrase is illustrated by the command to spend what one loves in order to attain righteousness.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:267#2/r10.claim: The produce from the earth means crops and fruits subject to zakat, which should also be given.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r11.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:267#2/r11.claim: Do not deliberately select inferior wealth, whether earned or grown; some interpret khabīth as unlawful wealth, but the first interpretation fits the comparison to something accepted only reluctantly.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r12.speaker: البراء بن عازب
TABRISI:2:267#2/r12.claim: One explanation of accepting it only with igmāḍ is that a creditor would take such an item from a debtor only by lenient accommodation.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r13.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:2:267#2/r13.claim: Another explanation is that one would accept it only by discounting its price; al-Ḥasan, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and al-Zajjāj are cited for this sense.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r14.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r14.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:267#2/r14.claim: God is independent of charity yet worthy of praise; hamīd may mean deserving praise, eliciting praise through gifts, or praising and rewarding donors, with the last fitting this context best.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r15.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r15.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:267#2/r15.claim: Hamīd suits this verse better than ḥalīm: after commanding the best earnings, God says He needs none of them yet praises those who obey and rewards their giving.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r2.speaker: عبيد بن رفاعة
TABRISI:2:267#2/r2.claim: A report from ʿUbayd b. Rifāʿa quotes the Prophet warning that merchants are sinners except those who are God-fearing, dutiful, truthful, and charitable.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r3.speaker: النبي
TABRISI:2:267#2/r3.claim: The Prophet is also quoted as saying that nine tenths of provision comes from trade and the remainder from seafaring.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r4.speaker: عائشة
TABRISI:2:267#2/r4.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports the Prophet saying that the best food a person eats is from his own earning, and that his child is part of his earning.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r5.speaker: النبي
TABRISI:2:267#2/r5.claim: A report through Saʿīd b. ʿUmayr quotes the Prophet saying that a person best earns through work by hand and every sound sale.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r6.speaker: علي
TABRISI:2:267#2/r6.claim: ʿAlī warns that anyone trading without knowledge becomes entangled in usury again and again.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r7.speaker: عبيدة السلماني
TABRISI:2:267#2/r7.claim: One view makes the command refer specifically to obligatory alms; this is attributed to ʿUbayda al-Salmānī and al-Ḥasan.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r8.speaker: الجبائي
TABRISI:2:267#2/r8.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī limits it to voluntary charity, since obligatory alms have a set value owed as a debt if underpaid, and even entirely poor-quality wealth may be used for zakat.

TABRISI:2:267#2/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267#2/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:267#2/r9.claim: The author prefers a general command covering obligatory and voluntary spending in every good cause; it also indicates that charity from earned lawful wealth brings greater reward because it costs more.

TABRISI:2:267/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267/r1.speaker: ابن كثير
TABRISI:2:267/r1.claim: Ibn Kathir reads the verb with a doubled tāʾ here and in thirty-one Qurʾanic places; the other readers use the lighter form.

TABRISI:2:267/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:267/r10.claim: The passage completes the prior discussion of spending by describing the gift and its recipient: believers are told to give charity while preserving it from invalidation by reproach or harm.

TABRISI:2:267/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267/r11.speaker: ابن مسعود
TABRISI:2:267/r11.claim: One explanation of good earnings is lawful income acquired through trade, reported from Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid.

TABRISI:2:267/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267/r12.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:267/r12.claim: Another explanation takes the phrase as the best and finest of what one has earned.

TABRISI:2:267/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:267/r2.claim: The two readings mean the same; the doubled form restores and assimilates the dropped tāʾ, while common recitation omits one of the two tāʾs for ease.

TABRISI:2:267/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:267/r3.claim: Tayammum means deliberately intending or aiming at something; Khifaf and al-Aʿshā use it this way, as do related forms for intending or being a target.

TABRISI:2:267/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:267/r4.claim: Khabīth means the defective or inferior thing; the dross expelled from silver and iron is called khabath, whose root sense is badness.

TABRISI:2:267/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:267/r5.claim: In trade, igmāḍ means accepting a reduced price for a defect; its root concerns concealment, with related senses of closing the eyes and sleep.

TABRISI:2:267/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267/r6.speaker: الفراء
TABRISI:2:267/r6.claim: Al-Farrāʾ construes an in illā an tughmiḍū as conditional: if you show some forbearance, you will take it, so the hamza is kasra.

TABRISI:2:267/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267/r7.speaker: المحققون
TABRISI:2:267/r7.claim: The leading grammarians reject the conditional analysis: an here is a verbal noun, meaning you would take it only through your forbearance.

TABRISI:2:267/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267/r8.speaker: أبو عبد الله
TABRISI:2:267/r8.claim: One reported occasion is people donating assets from pre-Islamic usury; they were forbidden to give these and commanded to give lawful, wholesome wealth.

TABRISI:2:267/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:267/r9.speaker: علي
TABRISI:2:267/r9.claim: Another occasion concerns people putting poor-quality dried dates into the charity dates; this is reported from ʿAlī, al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib, al-Ḥasan, and Qatāda.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r1.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r1.claim: Ansar hung their date harvest in the mosque for poor emigrants; some brought inferior bunches with shriveled or unripe dates, prompting the verse.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r2.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r2.claim: Another occasion report says the Prophet ordered zakat al-fitr and a man brought poor dates.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r3.speaker: عبيدة السلماني
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r3.claim: The commanded spending means obligatory charity, according to this view and others.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r4.claim: Another view takes the commanded spending as voluntary charity.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r5.claim: “Good things” means the best and finest goods.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r6.speaker: أبو معقل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p321#2/r6.claim: Another interpretation takes “good” as lawful goods.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r1.claim: Tayammamu means to seek or intend; the A'sha's line uses it for making one's way toward someone.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r2.speaker: الأعشى
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r2.claim: The poem's phrase tayaम्मamtu Qaysan witnesses the verb's meaning “I intended Qays.”

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r3.speaker: الأكثرون
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r3.claim: Khabith means low-quality produce; the occasion of revelation supports this interpretation.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r4.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r4.claim: Another view interprets khabith as unlawful property.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r5.claim: The verse's test is whether people would accept the inferior item as payment of a debt from one another, except by overlooking part of their due.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r6.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r6.claim: Ighmad means turning one's gaze away; lenient acceptance is called overlooking because a buyer asks the seller not to scrutinize the item.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r7.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p322/r7.claim: People also call leniency ighmad because a person closes his eyes to something displeasing and so overlooks it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p323/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p323/r1.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p323/r1.claim: God says He is rich to show that charity is not commanded from need; He remains praiseworthy.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p323/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p323/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p323/r2.claim: The root ghaniya means being self-sufficient or settling in a place that suffices; ghawani may denote women named for their beauty or husbands.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p323/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p323/r3.speaker: الخطابي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p323/r3.claim: Hamid means praised; the pattern fa'il here has a passive sense.

RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r1.claim: The preceding passage distinguished spending followed by reproach from sincere spending and supplied each type a clarifying parable; this verse specifies what kind of wealth to give.

RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r2.speaker: الحسن
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r2.claim: Al-Ḥasan takes the command to spend good things as obligatory alms; he argues that the imperative's apparent force is obligation.

RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r3.speaker: قوم
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r3.claim: Some authorities take the command as voluntary charity, citing reports of people donating their poorest produce and the revelation that followed.

RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r4.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب والحسن ومجاهد
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r4.claim: Reports say ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, and Mujāhid observed people giving inferior fruit and poor property as charity, prompting the verse.

RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that a man brought a bunch of spoiled dates for charity and the Prophet condemned the act before this verse was revealed.

RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r6.claim: Al-Rāzī says the command can cover both obligatory and voluntary giving because its wording urges action without specifying whether omission is permissible.

RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r7.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI-FULL:v7p53#2/r7.claim: If the command is obligatory, its general wording supports zakāt on all acquired assets and all crops, even small amounts; opponents restrict crops by reports excluding vegetables and yields below five wasqs.

RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r1.claim: Q 3:92 supports reading ṭayyib as valuable goods one likes to own, rather than worthless items one is eager to discard.

RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r2.speaker: القاضي
RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r2.claim: Al-Qāḍī argues quality alone cannot be intended, since that would require giving good property even if unlawful; he infers that ṭayyib means lawful.

RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r3.claim: Al-Rāzī proposes ṭayyib can convey both lawful and high quality through the shared idea of being agreeable to reason and religion or to inclination and desire.

RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r4.claim: For zakāt, all-good or all-poor holdings yield the corresponding share, while mixed holdings require a middle quality; the Prophet told Muʿādh not to take the best assets. Voluntary giving should be from one's best.

RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p54#2/r5.claim: Al-Rāzī asks what benefit the preposition min adds before the phrase about produce from the earth.

RAZI-FULL:v7p54/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p54/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p54/r1.claim: One view takes ṭayyib as good-quality property and khabīth as inferior property; another, held by Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid, takes them as lawful and unlawful.

RAZI-FULL:v7p54/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p54/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p54/r2.claim: The revelation context of people giving inferior goods supports the quality reading; moreover, unlawful property cannot normally be accepted even with indulgence, which challenges the lawful/unlawful reading.

RAZI-FULL:v7p54/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p54/r3.speaker: القفال
RAZI-FULL:v7p54/r3.claim: Al-Qaffāl answers that إغماض can mean leniency: the verse describes people willing to accept knowingly unlawful property by overlooking its source.

RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r1.claim: Ammamtuhu, yammamtuhu, and taʾammamtuhu all mean to aim at something; al-Aʿshā's verse illustrates the verb تيمم.

RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r2.speaker: ابن كثير
RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r2.claim: Ibn Kathīr doubles the tāʾ in تيمموا by assimilating the two original tāʾs; the other readers pronounce it lightly, with analogous variation elsewhere.

RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r3.speaker: أبو علي
RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r3.claim: Abū ʿAlī rejects this assimilation because a doubled initial consonant would require a wasl hamza, which is not used with the present tense.

RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r4.speaker: سيبويه والفراء
RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r4.claim: Authorities disagree about which tāʾ is deleted in the common light reading: Sībawayh says the second; al-Farrāʾ says either may be dropped because the remaining one represents it.

RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p55/r5.claim: One syntax ends the clause after ولا تيمموا الخبيث and makes منه تنفقون a rhetorical question; another leaves the clause open and supplies an omitted relative pronoun, as in al-Baqara 2:256.

RAZI-FULL:v7p56/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p56/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p56/r1.claim: إغماض literally means lowering or closing the eyes and is related to something hidden or subtle, such as obscure speech or a low-lying place.

RAZI-FULL:v7p56/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p56/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p56/r2.claim: One interpretation is accepting inferior goods only by lenience or embarrassment, as when a person closes his eyes to what he dislikes; the verse asks why donors offer God what they would not accept.

RAZI-FULL:v7p56/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p56/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p56/r3.claim: Another interpretation makes the donor compel the seller to close his eyes, meaning lower the price before the donor would accept the goods.

RAZI-FULL:v7p56/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p56/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p56/r4.claim: God needs no charity and is praised for explaining; alternatively, غني warns against giving inferior goods and حميد means He praises good deeds, as in Q 21:94.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r1.speaker: رسول الله
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r1.claim: The cited Prophetic report says children are among one's good earnings and permits eating from their property; no grading is stated.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r2.claim: What God brings from the earth includes three categories: plants, minerals, and buried treasure.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r3.speaker: عائشة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r3.claim: Aisha reports the Prophetic rule that crops below five wasqs owe no zakat; a wasq is sixty sāʿs, so the threshold is 300 sāʿs of wheat, barley, dates, or raisins; vegetables owe none.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r4.claim: Some invoke the verse's general wording to support Abu Hanifa's view that zakat applies to everything the earth produces, in any quantity and category; details are deferred to al-An'am.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r5.speaker: رسول الله
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r5.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that injury caused by an animal, a well, or a mine is uncompensated, while buried treasure owes one fifth.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r6.claim: The scholars infer that mines and buried treasure have different rules because the hadith separates them with a conjunction; otherwise it would have stated that the mine owes one fifth.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r7.claim: Rikaz linguistically and in the majority's legal usage is gold, silver, or gems embedded in the ground; an unworked nugget found inside a mine owes one fifth, while Malik's first and relied-upon view treats it like mined material requiring labor.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r8.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#2/r8.claim: A report asks the Prophet to define rikaz, and he calls it gold God placed in the earth when He created the heavens and earth; its transmitter Abdullah ibn Said is abandoned, and another route is unsound.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r1.claim: The transmitter Abdullah ibn Said is abandoned, and another route for the Abu Hurayra report is unsound, as al-Daraqutni notes.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r2.claim: Scholars agree that pre-Islamic buried wealth is rikaz; money buried after Islam is treated as lost property.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r3.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r3.claim: Malik assigns pre-Islamic treasure in certain Arab or peaceful Muslim lands to its finder with a fifth due; treasure in Islamic territory is lost property, conquest land belongs to its conquerors, and treaty land belongs to its residents, with another view giving it to all treaty residents.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r4.speaker: إسماعيل
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r4.claim: Ismail says treasure follows the spoils rule because a Muslim finds pagan property as if he had fought and seized it, receiving four fifths.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r5.speaker: ابن القاسم
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#3/r5.claim: Ibn al-Qasim recounts Malik changing his position on found objects such as jewelry, iron, and lead: one fifth, then none, and finally one fifth again.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r1.claim: The author says Malik’s final view that one fifth is due on found valuables is correct, supported by the general hadith and followed by most jurists.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r2.speaker: أبو حنيفة
