QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r2.claim: Abu Hanifa and Muhammad assign treasure found in a house to its owner, with a fifth due; Abu Yusuf and al-Thawri assign it to the finder. In open land all give it to the finder with a fifth, without distinguishing lands.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r3.claim: Some Medinese Malikites, al-Layth, Ibn Nafi, al-Shafi'i, and most scholars make no land-based distinction; the finder may keep the fifth if needy or give it to the poor.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r4.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r4.claim: Malik and his followers impose zakat on mined gold or silver once it reaches twenty mithqals or five awāq; additional extraction is counted while the vein continues, but a new vein starts a fresh assessment, due immediately like crops.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r5.speaker: سحنون
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r5.claim: Sahnun says a person's separate mines are not combined; each mine is assessed only when it independently reaches 200 dirhams or twenty dinars.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r6.speaker: محمد بن مسلمة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r6.claim: Ibn Maslama says separate mines are combined and assessed together, like crops.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r7.speaker: أبو حنيفة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r7.claim: Abu Hanifa and his companions treat minerals like rikaz: after a fifth, gold or silver is zakatable at the threshold after a year, combining with existing holdings; al-Thawri agrees.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r8.speaker: المزني
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r8.claim: Al-Muzani says al-Shafi'i hesitated over minerals but that his principles suggest treating extraction as a windfall, taxed after a year; al-Layth, al-Shafi'i as transmitted by al-Muzani, Dawud, and his followers hold this view.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r9.speaker: رسول الله
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#4/r9.claim: The jurists cite the hadith that newly acquired property owes no zakat until a year passes; al-Tirmidhi and al-Daraqutni transmit it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r1.speaker: رسول الله
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r1.claim: Al-Shafi'i cites a report from Abu Sa'id that the Prophet gave a small gold nugget in its soil to people whose hearts were to be reconciled, sent by Ali from Yemen; he takes this as evidence that mines follow zakat rules.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r2.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r2.claim: Malik cites a report that the Prophet granted Bilal ibn al-Harith the Qabaliyya mines, from which only zakat is still taken; its Rabi'a chain is disconnected and not acceptable to hadith specialists, though it is used as Medinese practice.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r3.speaker: البزار
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r3.claim: Al-Bazzar records a second grant version through al-Darawardi and another through Kathir ibn Abdullah describing the mines and cultivable land; the latter transmitter is widely judged weak.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r4.claim: The discussion of earth extraction is complete here; the sea's produce is treated in al-Nahl, and the animal-injury hadith is revisited in al-Anbiya.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r5.claim: Tayammum means to intend or aim; poetic evidence is deferred to al-Nisa, and the verse shows that earnings can be good or bad.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r6.speaker: أبو أمامة بن سهل
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r6.claim: Abu Umama ibn Sahl identifies the forbidden inferior dates as jaʿrūr and a variety called lawn ḥabīq; the Prophet prohibited taking them as zakat.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r7.speaker: رسول الله
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#5/r7.claim: In a report from Abu Umama's father, someone brought an inferior bunch of dates for charity; the Prophet asked who brought it, and the verse was revealed. The Prophet then barred jaʿrūr and ḥabīq dates from zakat.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r1.speaker: الزهري
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r1.claim: Al-Zuhri identifies the two forbidden types as varieties of dates from Medina; al-Tirmidhi transmits the al-Bara report and authenticates it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r2.claim: Al-Tabari and al-Nahhas report Ibn Masud's reading 'wa-la taʾammamū'; the author treats it as a dialectal variant.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r3.speaker: مسلم بن جندب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r3.claim: Muslim ibn Jundub reads the verb with a ḍamma on tāʾ and kasra on mīm; Ibn Kathir doubles tāʾ, and other authorities report further hamza and gemination variants.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r4.speaker: الجرجاني
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r4.claim: Al-Jurjani reports one parsing that ends the sentence at 'the bad'; 'from it you spend' then describes the inferior item and rebukes people for accepting it only by overlooking its defects.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r5.speaker: الجرجاني
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r5.claim: A second parsing keeps the sentence connected through 'from it'; the pronoun returns to earnings, and 'you spend' can be a circumstantial phrase.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r6.speaker: البراء بن عازب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r6.claim: Al-Bara, Ibn Abbas, and al-Dahhak say people would accept inferior goods in settling debts only by compromising their rights, so they should not offer God what they dislike for themselves.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r7.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r7.claim: Al-Hasan says people would buy the inferior item in the market only at a discount; Ali reportedly gives a similar explanation. Ibn Atiyya says these readings fit obligatory zakat.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r8.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r8.claim: Ibn al-Arabi argues that if the verse concerned obligatory zakat, inferior property could never be accepted even by compromise; only voluntary charity could be accepted without overlooking defects.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r9.speaker: البراء بن عازب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#6/r9.claim: Al-Bara also says a recipient would accept such a poor gift only out of embarrassment; Ibn Atiyya takes this as fitting voluntary charity. Ibn Zayd reads it as tolerating the reprehensibility of unlawful property.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r1.claim: The fragmentary verse says some people accept humiliation by overlooking a defect, supporting the lexical sense of lenience.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r10.claim: God is free of need for donations; whoever seeks reward should give something valuable, since the benefit is for the donor, and God is praised in every state.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r11.speaker: الزجاج
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r11.claim: Al-Zajjaj says God did not command charity out of need; He informed people that He is praiseworthy for all His blessings.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r2.claim: One proposed derivation of 'overlook' is closing one's eyes to something unpleasant, like the cited poet who says he shuts his eyes to troubling matters without being blind.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r3.claim: Another proposed derivation connects aghmada with going to an obscure place, as in expressions for traveling to Oman, Iraq, Najd, or Tihama; the phrase then implies interpretive effort to accept the item.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r4.speaker: الزهري
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r4.claim: Al-Zuhri has a light reading with fatḥa on tāʾ and kasra on mīm, and another doubled reading; the first suggests negotiating the price down and the second accepting at a discount, according to al-Nahhas and Abu Amr al-Dani.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r5.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r5.claim: Qatada is reported to read the verb with ḍamma on tāʾ, still ghayn, and light mīm, meaning that a discount is made for you; Ibn Jinni explains the form as finding oneself to have overlooked the matter.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r6.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r6.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the mainstream reading can mean either to excuse a defect, close the eye to it, or accept an obscure interpretation, whether the property is unlawful or an unwanted gift or debt payment.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r7.speaker: المهدوي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r7.claim: Al-Mahdawi says the reading means closing the eyes of one's insight to accepting the inferior item.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r8.speaker: الجوهري
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r8.claim: Al-Jawhari defines ghamḍ as leniency in buying or selling; 'make an allowance for me' asks the seller to lower the price because of poor quality.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267#7/r9.claim: The particle an is accusative here, with an implied meaning 'except by doing so.'

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r1.claim: The address to believers includes the entire community of Muhammad.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r2.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r2.claim: Ali, Ubayda al-Salmani, and Ibn Sirin say the command concerns obligatory zakat and forbids substituting inferior goods for good ones.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r3.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r3.claim: Ibn Atiyya says al-Bara, al-Hasan, and Qatada appear to understand voluntary charity, urging donors to choose good quality; the verse covers both obligatory and voluntary giving.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r4.claim: The obligatory view relies on the command's force and the specific ban on inferior goods, while the voluntary view says an imperative can recommend and inferior donations are also disfavored because God deserves the best.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r5.speaker: رسول الله
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r5.claim: Al-Bara reports that the Prophet saw someone hang a bunch of inferior dates and said, 'What a bad thing to hang'; the verse was then revealed. Al-Tirmidhi transmits it, with fuller wording deferred.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r6.speaker: ابن زيد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r6.claim: Ibn Zayd explains 'good things' as lawful earnings; most interpreters instead mean good and selected-quality property.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r7.claim: Earnings include wages from bodily labor and proceeds from trade; inheritance also counts as acquisition for the heir.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r8.speaker: ابن المبارك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r8.claim: Ibn Mubarak advises a person with sufficient subsistence to leave earning even for charitable ends, since earning and spending lawfully will both be questioned; abstaining from lawful gain is zuhd.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r9.speaker: ابن خويزمنداد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:267/r9.claim: Ibn Khuwiz Mindad says the verse permits a father to eat from his child's earnings, citing a Prophetic report continued in the next segment.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r1.claim: Give from what you earned that is lawful or choice quality, and from the wholesome crops, fruits, and minerals God brought forth for you.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r2.claim: Do not deliberately select the inferior portion of one's wealth or produce; several readings pronounce the initial t of tayammamu differently.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r3.claim: The phrase about spending is a prospective circumstantial clause; it may instead attach to minhu, with its pronoun referring to the inferior goods.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r4.claim: People would not accept inferior goods for their own dues unless they overlooked the defects; the wording derives from lowering one's gaze.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r5.claim: People used to give charity from defective dates and their worst produce, and were forbidden to do so.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:267/r6.claim: God needs no charity; He commands it for the donors' benefit and is praised for accepting and rewarding it.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r1.claim: Spend from good-quality earnings; this supports the obligation of zakat on trade goods.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r2.claim: What God brings from earth includes grain, fruit, and minerals; 'good things' is omitted because the preceding phrase already supplies it.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r3.claim: Do not deliberately choose inferior property to give; the phrase is circumstantial, describing one who intends to make that the expenditure.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r4.claim: You would accept such property for your own dues only by tolerating a concession; the idiom for overlooking one's right is likened to closing one's eyes.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r5.claim: People used to give poor dates and the worst dates as charity, and were forbidden to do so.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p131/r6.claim: God is independent of people's charity and worthy of praise.

QASHANI:2:266-267/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:266-267/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:266-267/r4.claim: The third kind is spending the best of one's earnings; one who chooses through God selects the finest through affinity with divine beauty.

QASHANI:2:266-267/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:266-267/r5.speaker: أمير المؤمنين علي عليه السلام
QASHANI:2:266-267/r5.claim: ʿAlī reports that God is beautiful and loves beauty, explaining the choice of the finest for charity.

QASHANI:2:266-267/r6.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:266-267/r6.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:266-267/r6.claim: An ego-centered donor cannot give the finest because the self hoards what it loves; this is not true righteousness, as the cited verse says.

QASHANI:2:266-267/r7.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:266-267/r7.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:266-267/r7.claim: Self-centered donors assign inferior goods to charity and would accept them only grudgingly, since they prefer their best possessions to God.

QASHANI:2:266-267/r8.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:266-267/r8.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:266-267/r8.claim: Recognizing God's independence means becoming rich through Him rather than money; His being praised means imitating His praiseworthy acts.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p674/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p674/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p674/r1.claim: The verb تيمم means to intend or aim; Arabic also has forms with hamza, and al-Khalil distinguishes aiming ahead from aiming from any direction.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p674/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p674/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p674/r2.claim: Khabith means bad or inferior and is the active participle of خبث, opposed to good.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p674/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p674/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p674/r3.claim: Ighmāḍ means tolerating or accepting less; it is related to lowering or closing the eye and to hidden or sunken things.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p674/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p674/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p674/r4.claim: Hamid means praised, a passive intensive form; its grammatical categories were discussed earlier in the sura.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p675/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p675/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p675/r1.claim: Niʿma is the fixed verb contrasted with biʾsa; its grammatical rules were discussed at 2:90.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p675/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p675/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p675/r8.claim: Reports give the occasion as people hanging date clusters in the mosque for the poor, then a Companion brought inferior dates believing it acceptable, after which the verse was revealed.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r1.speaker: علي وعبيدة السلماني وابن سيرين
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r1.claim: They apply the command to obligatory zakat, permit a small amount as voluntary charity, and take the command as obligatory.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r10.speaker: الراغب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r10.claim: He says earned wealth is singled out because people cling to it more than inherited wealth, so inherited property is implied by the wording.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r11.claim: Min is partitive; ma may be a relative pronoun with an omitted antecedent or a verbal noun interpreted as acquired property.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r2.speaker: البراء بن عازب والحسن وقتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r2.claim: They apply it to voluntary charity; the occasion supports recommending that voluntary gifts be of good quality.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r3.claim: The verse follows the preceding praise of spending and warning against reminders and ostentation by describing the quality of what is given.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r4.speaker: الأكثرون
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r4.claim: Most interpreters take good things as the best quality and khabith as inferior.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r5.speaker: ابن زيد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r5.claim: He interprets the good as lawful and the khabith as unlawful.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r6.speaker: علي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r6.claim: He identifies the good things as gold and silver.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r7.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r7.claim: He identifies them as trade assets.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r8.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r8.claim: He says tayyibat may simply urge spending from one's earnings; the word then describes the goodness of acquired wealth broadly, encompassing quality and lawfulness, supported by Ibn Mughaffal's statement that a believer's property has no khabith.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p676/r9.claim: What you earn includes anything obtained through one's work, bodily labor, or trade; another view includes inherited property as acquired by the predecessor.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r1.claim: The general command covers all good kinds of wealth while leaving required amounts unspecified, so it can support obligations for disputed categories such as trade goods, horses, children's wealth, jewelry, livestock, and debts.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r2.speaker: خويزمنداذ
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r2.claim: He infers that a father may eat from a child's property from a prophetic report calling children part of their parents' good earnings.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r3.speaker: عائشة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r3.claim: She reports the Prophet saying a person's best food is from his earnings and that his child is part of his earnings.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r4.claim: What God brings from the earth includes kinds of grains, fruits, minerals, and buried treasure; the wording expresses favor and recalls 2:29.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p677/r5.claim: The phrase omits tayyibat before what comes from the earth, supplied from context; repeating min emphasizes the command or signals another governing verb.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r1.claim: The poem says the initial tāʾ is lightened and discusses what follows when a long vowel precedes it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r10.claim: Tayyib and khabith are commonly substantives functioning as nouns; explicit descriptions are rarer, as in 24:26 and 7:157, and the prophetic refuge formula.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r2.claim: The author classifies these tāʾs by the sound immediately before them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r3.speaker: البزي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r3.claim: He notes Basran grammarians disallow some cases because they combine two unlicensed adjacent silent consonants.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r4.speaker: أبو ربيعة عن البزي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r4.claim: He also transmits a light tāʾ reading from al-Bazzi, like the other readers.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r5.speaker: سيبويه
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r5.claim: He disallows a still tāʾ in forms like يتكلمون because it would require a connecting alif, unavailable for a present verb; connection can make it possible, though Basran grammarians reject some adjacent-sukun cases.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r6.claim: He insists al-Bazzi's accepted reading is valid by transmission and says grammatical authority is not confined to Basran judgments.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r7.speaker: عبد الله
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r7.claim: He reads ولا تأمموا from أممت, meaning to intend.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r8.speaker: ابن عباس والزهري ومسلم بن جندب

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r9.speaker: الطبري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p678/r9.claim: He also records Abdullah reading ولا تأموا, with the same meaning of intending.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r1.claim: Some grammarians say the pronoun functions as an accusative object, while the author discusses whether the noun ending is dropped before it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r2.claim: The verse forbids deliberately choosing inferior property for charity; it does not forbid giving inferior goods when they are all one has or are not specially selected.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r3.claim: Wa lastum bi-ākhidhīhi may be an independent sentence or a circumstantial clause.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r4.speaker: البراء وابن عباس والضحاك وغيرهم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r4.claim: They explain that people would accept inferior goods for debts or rights only by yielding some of what was owed, so they should not give God what they would dislike receiving.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r5.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r5.claim: He says people would buy such goods in a market only at a reduced price; a similar report is related from Ali.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r6.speaker: البراء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r6.claim: He also explains that people would accept an inferior gift only out of embarrassment toward the giver.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r7.speaker: ابن زيد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r7.claim: He takes khabith as unlawful property which people would accept only while tolerating its unpleasantness.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r8.claim: The apparent wording broadly denies accepting inferior goods by any means, whether as a right or as a gift.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p680/r9.claim: The pronoun in بآخذيه is genitive by annexation although it functions semantically as an object; he rejects the claim that the noun's nūn is removed merely because a pronoun follows.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r1.claim: For إلا أن تغمضوا, some parse أن as accusative or genitive after an omitted preposition; al-Farraʾ gives a conditional sense, which Abu al-Abbas and others reject because أن is always open and verbal-noun forming.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r2.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r2.claim: They read تغمضوا from أغمض, with an omitted object such as eyes or insight, though it may be intransitive like أغضى.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r3.speaker: الزهري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r3.claim: He transmits a doubled-mīm reading and another variant with a different vowel pattern, both conveying the public reading's sense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r4.speaker: اليزيدي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r4.claim: The Yezidi form varies the verb vowels and means that one's judgment about it is obscured.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r5.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r5.claim: He reads the mīm doubled and open.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r6.speaker: قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r6.claim: He reads the verb with ḍamma on tāʾ and fatḥa on mīm, lightly pronounced, meaning that the giver lets the recipient tolerate it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r7.speaker: أبو الفتح
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r7.claim: He explains Qatada's reading as finding people already tolerant of the matter, or entering into it and being drawn toward it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r8.claim: God is independent of charity; the charity's benefit returns to its giver, and God deserves praise in every state.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r9.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p681/r9.claim: Hasan says God draws praise from creation by granting them blessings; another view says He deserves praise for prescribing worship.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r1.claim: The majority read تيمموا, dropping one of the two original tāʾs for ease; the earlier discussion is at 2:85.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r2.speaker: البزي
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r2.claim: Al-Bazzī doubles the tāʾ by assimilating the first into the second; this is allowed because the first quiescent segment is weak, unlike his readings at 92:14 and 24:15.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس والزهري
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Zuhrī read تيممو with different vowels, treating it as the unabridged form of يمم.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r4.speaker: عبد الله
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r4.claim: A reading attributed to ʿAbd Allāh is تؤمموا, from أممت, ‘I intended.’

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r5.speaker: الخليل
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r5.claim: تيمم means intend; forms include أمم, يمم, تيمم, and تأمم. Al-Khalīl distinguishes intending what is ahead from intending something from any direction.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#2/r6.claim: الطيب and الخبيث are substantivized adjectives, as in 24:26 and 7:157; the passage also cites the prophetic phrase من الخبث والخبائث.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r1.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r1.claim: منه تنفقون may be circumstantial from the subject of تيمموا: ‘do not aim at the bad while spending from it’; this is anticipated because spending follows aiming.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r2.claim: A second circumstantial analysis attaches the clause to الخبيث, whose pronoun is resumed in منه.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r3.claim: A third reading treats تنفقون منه as a new statement after a pause; despite its reproachful tone, the author says the sense rules it out.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r4.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r4.claim: ولستم بآخذيه may be independent; it may instead be circumstantial, especially if the preceding command is treated as complete.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#3/r5.claim: The suffix in بآخذيه is either genitive in form despite functioning as an object, or accusative as al-Akhfash argues; Hishām allows tanwin before an attached pronoun, supported by poetic examples.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r1.claim: إلا أن تغمضوا derives from إلا بأن with the preposition omitted, leaving disagreement over genitive or accusative; the bāʾ attaches to تيمموا or بآخذيه.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r2.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r2.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ allows a circumstantial sense from أخذ, ‘you take it only while overlooking’; Sībawayh does not allow أن plus its clause in this role.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r3.speaker: الفراء
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r3.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reads the construction conditionally, ‘if you overlook it, you take it’; the author says this analysis has been rejected in grammar works and compares 2:229 and 2:237.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r4.claim: The common reading تغمضوا has two senses: omitted ‘eyes or insight,’ or a metaphorical intransitive meaning ‘lower your gaze/tolerate.’

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r5.speaker: الزهري
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r5.claim: Al-Zuhrī reads a doubled form with a distinct vowel pattern; he also has a form from غمض, a dialect equivalent of أغمض.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r6.speaker: اليزيدي
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r6.claim: Al-Yazīdī reads تغمضوا from غمض يغمض, ‘its judgment was obscure to you.’

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r7.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r7.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda have passive forms meaning that people are made to tolerate or overlook it; Qatāda lightens the doubled mīm.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r8.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:267#4/r8.claim: For Qatāda’s form Abū al-Baqāʾ allows a sense like ‘you find it in that state,’ as in أحمدت الرجل; another gloss is entering into it and being drawn toward it.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:267/r1.claim: The object of أنفقوا may be من’s object, partitive ‘spend some provision,’ or an omitted noun such as شيئا; ما is relative with omitted suffix or a verbal noun interpreted as مكسوبكم, and the relative analysis is better.

SAMIN-DURR:2:267/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:267/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:267/r2.claim: مما أخرجنا coordinates with the earlier phrase through repeated من, for emphasis or a new implied أنفقوا; طيبات is understood, لكم depends on أخرجنا with causal لام, and من الأرض marks origin.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697#2/r1.speaker: الحاكم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697#2/r1.claim: Al-Hakim grades the al-Bara report sound according to Muslim’s criteria, though Muslim did not include it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697#2/r2.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697#2/r2.claim: Al-Bara’s fuller account describes people of the Suffa striking hanging date clusters and some donors mixing in worthless dates; after the verse, they brought good dates.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697#2/r3.speaker: الترمذي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697#2/r3.claim: Al-Tirmidhi calls this fuller al-Bara report hasan gharib.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697#2/r4.speaker: أبو أمامة بن سهل بن حنيف عن أبيه
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697#2/r4.claim: A report from Sahl says the Prophet forbade two inferior date varieties because people were selecting poor fruit for charity; Abu Dawud’s wording explicitly says they were not to be taken as zakat.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r1.claim: The command to spend from good things means giving charity from the good wealth God has provided.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r2.claim: Mujahid identifies earnings as trade made possible by God.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r3.speaker: علي والسدي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r3.claim: Ali and al-Suddi explain earnings as gold and silver, alongside fruits and crops grown from the earth.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says to give the best, finest, and most valuable wealth, not its inferior portion, since God accepts only what is good.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r5.claim: The verb تيمموا means intend or aim for the bad; recipients would accept it only by overlooking its defect, so believers should not offer God what they dislike.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r6.claim: An alternate interpretation forbids turning away from lawful wealth to spend what was acquired unlawfully.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r7.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r7.claim: A report from Ibn Masud says forbidden earnings are not blessed or accepted as charity, and evil is erased by good rather than by more evil.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r8.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r8.claim: Ibn Kathir prefers the first interpretation, that the verse prohibits giving inferior goods; al-Bara reports its revelation amid the Ansar’s charity of dates.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r9.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r9.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p697/r9.claim: Al-Bara says the verse was revealed after some Ansar hung poor-quality dates among their contributions for poor Muhajirun at the Prophet’s mosque.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r1.speaker: النسائي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r1.claim: Al-Nasa'i transmits the Sahl report through Abu Umama without naming Sahl as an intermediary; Ibn Wahb also transmits it that way.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن معقل
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r2.claim: Ibn Ma'qil says a Muslim’s earnings are not intrinsically bad, but one should not give rotten dates, counterfeit coins, or anything worthless.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r3.speaker: عائشة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r3.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet neither ate nor prohibited eating monitor lizard, but said not to feed the poor what one would not eat.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r4.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r4.claim: Al-Bara explains that a creditor would reject inferior payment unless he accepted it as a shortfall from his due.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p698/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas compares the command to a creditor refusing less than the full amount of a right, asking how people can offer God what they would not accept; Ibn Jarir links this to spending what one loves.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p699/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p699/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p699/r1.claim: God needs no charity; He commands good giving to equalize rich and poor, while all creation depends on His inexhaustible bounty.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p699/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p699/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p699/r2.claim: God is praiseworthy in all His actions, words, law, and decree; pure giving earns generous multiplied reward.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r1.claim: The command to spend follows the command to act rightly: spending from good earnings affirms faith, and purifying one's gift has the broader benefit.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r10.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r10.claim: God rewards a good giver abundantly; He has always been and remains praiseworthy, whether His decree accords with human preference or not.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r11.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r11.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r11.claim: Hamid is an intensive form from praise, which is God's even, unvarying order whether it pleases human souls or opposes them.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r2.claim: Trade profits and produce are both blessings created from the earth; this should encourage generous giving of the best lawful goods and deter miserliness or giving illicit goods.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r3.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r3.claim: The address to those earning through their labor suggests the Emigrants, followed by those giving from crops and cultivation, suggesting the Helpers.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r4.claim: Tayyammamu means deliberately undertaking to target the bad portion for giving.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r5.claim: Khabith is an intensive form: what the soul finds repellent outwardly and inwardly, opposite the good that it welcomes.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r6.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r6.claim: The construction implies giving only the bad, extending the prohibition even to one who gives both good and bad but does not single out the bad.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r7.claim: The test is whether a giver would accept the inferior property from someone who owed him; one would take it only by overlooking its defect reluctantly.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r8.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r8.claim: Ighmad is to avert one's gaze from a defect; its root evokes a sleep that veils the senses and then clears.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r9.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p521/r9.claim: God is wholly perfect and rich: He needs neither poor-quality gifts nor spending itself; the command is kindness to people, for reward and punishment.

DURR-FULL:v2p48/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r7.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r7.claim: The good earnings include gold and silver; what God brings from earth includes grain, dates, and everything liable to zakat.

DURR-FULL:v2p50/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r1.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r1.claim: What people earn means trade; what God brings from earth means fruits.

DURR-FULL:v2p50/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r2.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r2.claim: The Prophet sets zakat thresholds at five wasqs of dates, five awaq of silver, and five camels; a Muslim wording extends the first threshold to grain and dates.

DURR-FULL:v2p50/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r3.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r3.claim: The Prophet gives the same minimums for silver, camels, and dates before zakat is due.

DURR-FULL:v2p50/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r4.speaker: ابن عمر
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r4.claim: Produce watered by rain, springs, or natural moisture owes a tenth; produce watered by laborious irrigation owes half a tenth.

DURR-FULL:v2p50/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r5.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r5.claim: The Prophet sets a tenth on produce watered by rivers and springs and half a tenth on produce watered by a water-lifting device.

DURR-FULL:v2p50/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r6.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r6.claim: The Prophet repeats the tenth for rain or spring water and half a tenth for laborious irrigation.

DURR-FULL:v2p50/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r7.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r7.claim: The Prophet waived zakat on horses and slaves, set one dirham per forty dirhams of silver, none at 190, and five at 200.

DURR-FULL:v2p50/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r8.speaker: أبو ذر
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r8.claim: A report says zakat is due on camels, cattle, sheep, and bazz (cloth).

DURR-FULL:v2p50/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r9.speaker: سمرة
DURR-FULL:v2p50/r9.claim: The Prophet ordered zakat on property kept for sale.

DURR-FULL:v2p57/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p57/r1.speaker: بلال بن الحارث
DURR-FULL:v2p57/r1.claim: The Prophet collected zakat from the Qabaliyya mines.

DURR-FULL:v2p57/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p57/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p57/r2.claim: Amber is something cast ashore by the sea, and if it contains something valuable, one fifth is due.

DURR-FULL:v2p57/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p57/r5.speaker: جابر
DURR-FULL:v2p57/r5.claim: The Prophet set one dinar of zakat on each freely grazing horse.

DURR-FULL:v2p57/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p57/r6.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v2p57/r6.claim: The Prophet says there is no zakat on a Muslim's slave or horse, except the zakat of breaking the fast on slaves.

DURR-FULL:v2p57/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p57/r7.speaker: البراء بن عازب
DURR-FULL:v2p57/r7.claim: Among the Ansar, date bunches were hung in the mosque for the poor; some offered inferior or broken dates, prompting the command to give good produce, which recipients themselves would accept only reluctantly.

DURR-FULL:v2p57/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p57/r8.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v2p57/r8.claim: Some owners selected dates from their poorer garden and mixed in chaff for charity, prompting the revelation.

DURR-FULL:v2p58/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p58/r1.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v2p58/r1.claim: When zakat was required, some hypocrites brought their worst fruit as charity, and the verse forbade this.

DURR-FULL:v2p58/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p58/r2.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
DURR-FULL:v2p58/r2.claim: When a man brought poor dates for the commanded zakat al-fitr, the Prophet told the date assessor not to accept them, and the verse followed.

DURR-FULL:v2p58/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p58/r3.speaker: جابر
DURR-FULL:v2p58/r3.claim: For zakat al-fitr, the Prophet told Abdullah ibn Rawaha not to assess poor dates brought by a man; the verse followed.

DURR-FULL:v2p58/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p58/r4.speaker: سهل بن حنيف
DURR-FULL:v2p58/r4.claim: A man brought inferior date bunches for charity; the Prophet asked who brought them, and the verse followed. He barred two named poor date varieties from zakat.

DURR-FULL:v2p58/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p58/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p58/r5.claim: Some Companions bought cheap food to give as charity, prompting the verse.

DURR-FULL:v2p58/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p58/r6.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
DURR-FULL:v2p58/r6.claim: Ali says the verse concerns obligatory zakat: people kept the good dates and gave the poor ones to the collector.

DURR-FULL:v2p59/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r1.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r1.claim: The poor-quality date should not be offered for zakat unless the recipient accepts a discounted value.

DURR-FULL:v2p59/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r2.speaker: عطاء
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r2.claim: When someone hung dried, poor dates among date bunches, the Prophet condemned it and the verse followed.

DURR-FULL:v2p59/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r3.speaker: محمد بن يحيى بن حبان
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r3.claim: A man brought several known inferior date varieties as zakat; God and the Messenger rejected them and the verse followed.

DURR-FULL:v2p59/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r4.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r4.claim: People gave dried chaff and the worst dates, so they were forbidden and ordered to give good produce.

DURR-FULL:v2p59/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r5.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r5.claim: People gave the dregs of their property, prompting the prohibition.

DURR-FULL:v2p59/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r6.speaker: عوف بن مالك
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r6.claim: The Prophet poked a hanging date bunch containing chaff and asked why its owner had not given better dates; he would eat the chaff at resurrection.

DURR-FULL:v2p59/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p59/r7.claim: Give the best and most prized property; a person would reject an inferior repayment unless discounting its value, so should not offer it to God; he cites 3:92.

DURR-FULL:v2p60/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن مغفل
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r1.claim: A Muslim's earnings are not intrinsically bad, but charity should not be dried chaff, counterfeit money, or something worthless; the exception means not to overlook it.

DURR-FULL:v2p60/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r2.speaker: البراء بن عازب
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r2.claim: Do not deliberately select poor produce for charity; God has no need of your charity.

DURR-FULL:v2p60/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r3.claim: He tells Ibn al-Azraq that the command means not to choose the worst fruits or crops for charity, which one would not accept oneself; al-A'sha's poetry illustrates the verb aim.

DURR-FULL:v2p60/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r4.speaker: عبيدة
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r4.claim: The rule concerns obligatory zakat; for voluntary charity, giving a counterfeit dirham may be acceptable if it is better than a date.

DURR-FULL:v2p60/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r5.claim: People gave dried dates as zakat; a creditor would accept such repayment only by overlooking part of what was owed.

DURR-FULL:v2p60/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r6.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r6.claim: A creditor or buyer would accept inferior dates only for an extra quantity over good dates; all charity should be good.

DURR-FULL:v2p60/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r7.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r7.claim: Khabith includes poor dates and grain; accepting counterfeit dirhams for a debt means overlooking part of one's claim.

DURR-FULL:v2p60/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r8.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v2p60/r8.claim: A person would not accept an inferior item in the market unless its price were reduced.

DURR-FULL:v2p61/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p61/r1.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v2p61/r1.claim: You would not accept less than your due from a debtor, so do not offer God your worst property.

DURR-FULL:v2p61/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p61/r2.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v2p61/r2.claim: One would not accept poor dates at the price of good dates unless the price were discounted.

DURR-FULL:v2p61/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p61/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن معاوية الفاخري
DURR-FULL:v2p61/r3.claim: The Prophet says faith's flavor includes worshipping God alone and paying annual zakat willingly from average property, not the worst or best.

DURR-FULL:v2p61/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p61/r4.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
DURR-FULL:v2p61/r4.claim: Umar instructed the Taif collector to leave pregnant, milk-bearing, breeding, and other premium livestock, taking middle-value animals as fair between poor and good stock.

DURR-FULL:v2p61/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p61/r5.speaker: سعر
DURR-FULL:v2p61/r5.claim: Two collectors refused a pregnant sheep because the Prophet forbade taking one, then accepted an average sheep.

DURR-FULL:v2p61/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p61/r6.speaker: أبي بن كعب
DURR-FULL:v2p61/r6.claim: The Prophet's collector refused an owner's superior camel in place of the assessed young camel; when the owner offered it voluntarily, the Prophet accepted it and prayed for blessing.

DURR-FULL:v2p62/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r1.claim: The Prophet accepts the owner's voluntary better camel, promises reward, and prays for blessing.

DURR-FULL:v2p62/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r10.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r10.claim: Paying zakat fulfills one's duty, but charity from unlawfully acquired wealth earns no reward and leaves its sin with the giver.

DURR-FULL:v2p62/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r11.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r11.claim: Giving zakat cannot make unlawful earnings pure, and withholding zakat corrupts otherwise good earnings.

DURR-FULL:v2p62/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r12.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r12.claim: The heavenly response to pilgrimage depends on lawful provision: lawful food and transport bring a blessed pilgrimage; unlawful provision is rejected and makes it blameworthy.

DURR-FULL:v2p62/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r2.claim: A good dirham is dearer to him than one hundred thousand; he invokes the command to give from good earnings.

DURR-FULL:v2p62/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r6.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r6.claim: Unlawful wealth spent in charity is not blessed or accepted and becomes provision for the Fire; evil is erased only by good.

DURR-FULL:v2p62/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r7.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r7.claim: A separate report says evil cannot expiate evil, while good can expiate evil.

DURR-FULL:v2p62/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r8.speaker: ابن عمر
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r8.claim: When earnings are pure, charity is purified; evil cannot expiate evil.

DURR-FULL:v2p62/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r9.speaker: أبو الدرداء
DURR-FULL:v2p62/r9.claim: Unlawful earnings used even for good ends remain a grave sickness; lawful earnings used rightly wash away sins like water washes dust from stone.

DURR-FULL:v2p64/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r1.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r1.claim: Hasan says a man may take what he wishes from his son's property, including a concubine; Qatada says he disliked the latter ruling.

DURR-FULL:v2p64/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r2.speaker: الزهري
DURR-FULL:v2p64/r2.claim: A needy mother of an orphan may be supported from the child's property and manage it with him; a wealthy mother has no share.

BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r1.claim: Ṭayyib can mean lawful or good-quality earnings; the command excludes unlawful giving while ‘spend what you love’ supports the quality reading.

BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r2.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī's Kashshāf glosses ṭayyib as the best of one's earnings.

BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r3.speaker: بعض الأفاضل
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r3.claim: Some scholars prefer ‘good-quality’ over ‘lawful’: the command already excludes unlawful gifts, and khabīth below means inferior.

BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r4.claim: The earth's produce includes grains, fruits, and minerals; taya mmu means to aim for, and khabīth means inferior or base.

BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r5.claim: Ṭayyib and khabīth each have three senses: lawful and forbidden, pure and impure, or pleasing and repugnant to natural taste.

BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r6.claim: The preposed phrase restricts the prohibited practice: do not target inferior goods as the sole charity; the wording censures that habit.

BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says people used to give away rotten and inferior dates, which they were forbidden to do.

BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r8.claim: People would not accept inferior goods in a transaction except reluctantly, such as taking poor property for a sound debt for fear of losing the claim or from need.

BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p350#2/r9.claim: The idiom ‘overlook’ asks a seller not to press every detail, as if he were looking away; God is self-sufficient and commands giving for donors' benefit.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r1.claim: The command covers good or lawful earnings, including currency, trade goods, and livestock; earthly produce forms a separate category.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r10.claim: The parse making an as-clause a circumstantial modifier conflicts with Sībawayh, and al-Farrāʾ’s conditional reading should be rejected; a remote alternative divides the phrase into a rebuke and question.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r11.claim: God needs no gifts and ordered them for donors’ benefit; giving inferior goods shows ignorance of His greatness, while gratitude entails selecting good gifts.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r12.claim: The verse is used to argue that land produce, even small crops and vegetables, owes zakat; a tenant farmer pays it, and a creditor need not accept defective goods instead of sound payment.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r2.speaker: علي
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r2.claim: In a report from Ibn Jarīr, ʿAlī says earned good things are gold and silver, while God’s produce includes grain, dates, and everything subject to zakat.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r3.claim: Repeating min marks two independently valid sources of giving, or serves for emphasis, which the author regards as more likely.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r4.claim: The clause describes what may be given, after the passage explained the basic obligation and manner of spending.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r5.claim: Tayammamū means deliberately aim at something; one of its two initial tāʾs is dropped, and reading variants by ʿAbd Allāh and Ibn ʿAbbās carry the same meaning.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r6.claim: Khabīth means defective or poor quality and functions as a substantive adjective; preposing ‘from it you spend’ restricts attention to their practice of donating inferior goods.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r7.speaker: عبيدة السلماني
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r7.claim: ʿUbayda al-Salmānī says ʿAlī explained that the verse concerns obligatory zakat: harvesters saved their good dates and gave poor-quality dates to the collector.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r8.claim: The phrase says donors would take such inferior goods only by overlooking their defects; accepting them is like closing one’s eyes or tolerating a flaw.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r9.speaker: الزهرى، قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#3/r9.claim: Al-Zuhrī intensifies the mīm or varies its vowel; Qatāda reads a passive form meaning donors are made to overlook the defects.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r1.claim: Reports say some people hung date clusters in the mosque for the needy, while others brought spoiled inferior fruit thinking this was acceptable; the verse then came down.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r10.claim: The prohibition is binding in obligatory dues and expresses dislike, whether prohibitive or mild, in voluntary gifts; its general force includes both.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r11.claim: The verse appears to cover all wealth but leaves the threshold, amount, and scope by property class unspecified; Prophetic practice and hadith clarify these, with details left to legal manuals.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r12.claim: God commands spending from pure earnings and produce rather than inferior goods one would refuse oneself.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r13.claim: God is self-sufficient, so charity benefits its giver; as Praiseworthy, He also rewards good works with greater favor and appreciates efforts made for Him.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r2.claim: Obligatory dues are paid in the same class as the property: gold for gold, silver for silver, money for money, each animal kind for itself, and each crop for itself.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r3.claim: A payer may convert lower-quality goods into the higher quality owed and pay their value at their discretion, but the due itself is not to be inferior.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r4.claim: Paying dues in kind is the easiest method and, by applying God's law of ease, benefited Islam's spread and the promotion of justice.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r5.claim: This system's public benefits depend on pious, ethical officials who guard entrusted property more carefully than their own.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r6.claim: With trustworthy administration, much wealth can meet public needs directly and necessary exchanges can be conducted soundly, reducing expenses and expanding public resources.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r7.claim: When officials and the public are immoral and entrusted funds are misused, concealed, stolen, or wasted, governments shift toward cash taxes; costs and burdens rise, money dominates, intermediaries profit, and producers' future is threatened.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r8.claim: Mismanagement and lack of religious duty cause social calamity; those who reject this divine command act against wisdom and ruin their future however learned they claim to be.

ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271#2/r9.claim: The ruling's scope over voluntary charity is debated: unlawful wealth cannot be given voluntarily for divine reward, though inferior-quality lawful wealth may be given.

ELMALILI:2:267-271/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r1.claim: Two primary sources of wealth are acquisition through work and what God brings forth from the earth, including crops, fruits, minerals, and buried treasure.

ELMALILI:2:267-271/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r10.claim: When money and capital become absolute rulers, workers' reaction produces conflict between labor and capital and disrupts social order.

ELMALILI:2:267-271/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r2.claim: Acquisition can mean obtaining wealth through work, craft, or contract, directly or indirectly, or ownership accruing over something; the latter also includes inheritance.

ELMALILI:2:267-271/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r3.claim: Earth here includes land, sea, and air, while mixed products are assigned to whichever of work or natural production predominates.

ELMALILI:2:267-271/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r4.claim: Work is the nearer cause and often precedes extraction from the earth, yet depends on created faculties and resources; acquisition can never be independent, whereas the earth may be.

ELMALILI:2:267-271/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r5.claim: Workers err when they treat labor as the sole cause of wealth and capital as worthless, overlooking that labor's value is tied to the capital it produces.

ELMALILI:2:267-271/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r6.claim: Capital can facilitate and multiply later work, so hostility to it amounts to wishing for workers' own hardship and deprivation.

ELMALILI:2:267-271/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r7.claim: Capital owners make the opposite error when they treat money as an absolute cause, disregard labor, and seek to benefit from others' work without working themselves.

ELMALILI:2:267-271/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r8.claim: Money in a safe feeds no one without labor; money is itself an output of past work, and exploiting labor destroys the foundation on which capitalists depend.

ELMALILI:2:267-271/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:267-271/r9.claim: The true original capital is the earth and creation's gifts; money is only a result of labor and can serve as a means to facilitate further work.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p55/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p55/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p55/r2.claim: The command to spend is delayed until after admonition, encouragement, and warning; this rhetorical ordering prepares acceptance because charity was already a familiar religious duty deserving careful praise and correction.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p55/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p55/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p55/r3.claim: A sermon attributed to ʿAlī exhorts people to fight after Sufyān al-Ghāmidī's raid on al-Anbār and killing its governor; Ibn ʿĀshūr suspects jihad was altered from qitāl by an interpolator or mistake, since the context says fighting and he doubts ʿAlī said the transmitted word.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r1.claim: تيمموا derives from تتيمموا with one imperfect prefix t dropped and means intend or deliberately seek.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r2.claim: Khabīth means the worst in a class, used of unlawful or impure things and the opposite extreme of good; its use in a prohibition covers every kind it denotes.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r3.claim: The fronted منه in the circumstantial phrase implies exclusive targeting: do not give only inferior property; mixed property is permitted, especially for zakāt distributed across the same asset class, while livestock is assessed at average quality.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r4.claim: In a report from the Muwaṭṭaʾ, the Prophet tells a collector who brought premium dates to sell inferior dates for dirhams and then buy premium ones, showing that zakāt is collected from each class of its own kind.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56#2/r5.claim: Most readers pronounce تيمموا with one light t in connected and initial reading; al-Bazzī from Ibn Kathīr doubles it in connected reading.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r1.claim: The command may require obligatory zakāt, recommend voluntary charity, or encompass both as a shared request; other evidence determines each ruling, and the qualifier good property fits all spending.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r2.claim: Good things means the best of each asset class, and also lawfully earned wealth; prophetic reports say God accepts only what is pure. The land-produced category needs no repeated qualifier because cultivation implies lawful effort.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r3.claim: The Prophet says the Merciful receives charity from pure earnings, and another report states that God is pure and accepts only what is pure.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r4.claim: Produce from the earth means crops and fruit, whether naturally grown or produced through ordinary causes such as irrigation and planting.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p56/r5.claim: Some include minerals: Mālik requires zakāt at the threshold at one-fortieth, while Abū Ḥanīfa treats minerals as non-zakāt wealth subject to one-fifth; some include buried treasure, taxed at one-fifth as booty under Mālikī law. Ibn ʿĀshūr suggests the verse likely means monetary and livestock zakāt alongside crops and fruit.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r1.claim: The clause may be a statement used as an argument against giving unlawful property: just as people dislike acquiring it, they should dislike giving it; alternatively, it is a prohibition against accepting known unlawful property, which does not become lawful by transfer. Both readings imply that known unlawful wealth may not be taken.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r2.claim: إغماض literally means closing an eyelid and figuratively can mean ease or rest; al-Aʿshā's phrase فاغتمضي means be content or at ease.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r3.claim: Because closing the eyes prevents seeing, إغماض can mean tolerating an objectionable thing; al-Ṭirimmāḥ uses it for people accepting humiliation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r4.claim: The phrase أغمض عينه على قذى describes deliberately overlooking a severe annoyance; a poem by ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Zurāra al-Kilābī illustrates enduring it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p57/r5.claim: On the declarative reading, the exception restricts the negation; on the prohibitive reading, it intensifies the prohibition by seeming to allow acceptance only if one disregards the rule.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p58/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p58/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p58/r1.claim: The conclusion reminds people that God needs no donations that fail to help the poor or tolerate the unlawful, yet praises those who give pure charity; أَعْلَموا draws attention or addresses those acting as if unaware.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p58/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p58/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p58/r2.claim: God's absolute richness means one should offer Him the best, just as one would give the best to someone who needs nothing.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p58/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p58/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p58/r3.claim: Ḥamīd may be an intensive active adjective because God greatly praises good-doers, or passive meaning praised; believers should be free of stinginess and thanked for pure charity.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r7.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب عليه السلام
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r7.claim: Al-Durr al-Manthūr reports ʿAlī explaining good earnings as gold and silver, and earthly produce as grain, dates, and everything subject to zakat.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r8.speaker: البراء بن عازب
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r8.claim: Al-Barāʾ reports that the verse was revealed about some Anṣār who hung poor clusters of dates for the hungry Ahl al-Ṣuffa; after the warning, they brought their good dates instead. Al-Tirmidhī's report is authenticated.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#8/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#8/r1.speaker: الصادق عليه السلام
TABATABAI:2:261-274#8/r1.claim: A report in al-Kāfī says some gave the worst dates, jaʿrūr and maʿāfāra, as zakat from good palms; the Prophet told them not to estimate those palms or bring their produce, and explained accepting such fruit would mean overlooking its defects.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#8/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#8/r2.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:2:261-274#8/r2.claim: Another report says people who acquired ill-gotten wealth in the pre-Islamic period wanted to donate it after Islam, but God required them to give from the best of their earnings.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.claim: The connected themes suggest this passage was revealed as one unit: spending grows seven hundredfold or more, sincere giving bears fruit, ostentation and reminders or harm ruin reward, good wealth should be given, the poor detained in God's path are recipients, and the reward is great.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.claim: The passage orders its teaching around purpose (giving for God, not people), manner (without reproach or injury), quality (good rather than bad wealth), recipient (the needy constrained in God's path), and reward.

TABATABAI:2:266-267/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r10.claim: The ending either tells donors to consider that God praises good giving despite His wealth, or that a rich and praiseworthy God should not be approached with an unworthy gift.

TABATABAI:2:266-267/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r7.claim: Tayammum means intending, khabīth is the opposite of good, and the grammatical circumstantial clauses attach respectively to the subjects of 'intend' and 'spend'.

TABATABAI:2:266-267/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r8.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r8.claim: The exception means that people would accept such poor produce only while overlooking its defects, or while bearing the discomfort of doing so.

TABATABAI:2:266-267/r9.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r9.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r9.claim: God requires good earnings, not the worthless property one would reluctantly accept; giving the latter looks like disposal rather than generosity and cultivates neither affection nor virtue.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:267/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:267/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:267/r1.claim: After explaining the purpose and manner of giving, the text commands that charity come from good rather than bad produce and goods.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:267/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:267/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:267/r2.claim: Some take the command to give good goods as binding and identify the charity as zakat, which must not be paid from inferior property; others say it concerns voluntary charity, making the command advisory.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:267/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:267/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:267/r3.claim: Some understand tayyibat as lawful; the author says good-quality and lawful meanings do not conflict and prefers including both.

QIRAAT-ER:2:267:18#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:2:267:18#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:2:267:18#1/r1.claim: Assimilation of initial tāʾ is a phonological variant with no semantic change.

STUDYQURAN:2:267/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r1.claim: The call to give from good things echoes the Quranic statement that piety requires spending from what one loves.

STUDYQURAN:2:267/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r2.speaker: Prophet
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r2.claim: A famous hadith says belief is incomplete until one wants for a neighbor, or in another version a brother, what one wants for oneself.

STUDYQURAN:2:267/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r3.claim: Good things may mean wholesome and desirable items one would not reject, or things that are lawful.

STUDYQURAN:2:267/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r4.claim: Charity should not be funded with unlawful or distasteful things.

STUDYQURAN:2:267/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r5.claim: A report says Companions hung good dates in the mosque for the poor; another group brought inferior dates, and the verse was said to have been revealed then.

STUDYQURAN:2:267/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r6.claim: A hadith says God apportions worldly provision to people regardless of His love, but grants religion only to those He loves.

STUDYQURAN:2:267/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r7.claim: The same hadith says true submission requires heart and tongue submission and believers’ body parts being safe from lies and wrongdoing.

STUDYQURAN:2:267/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r8.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:267/r8.claim: The hadith says charity from unlawfully earned wealth is not accepted, wrongdoing is erased by good rather than more wrongdoing, and one should not feed others what one would not eat.
